en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta was a frequent visitor to a certain family and had been provided with a regular meal there.
Whatever fresh or cooked food arose in that family, a portion was set aside for the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta.
Now on that occasion, meat had arisen in that family in the evening.
Then a portion was set aside for the Venerable Upananda of the Sakyan clan.
At the time of dawn, a young boy from that family woke up and cried out, “Give me meat!
Then that man said to his wife, “Give the portion belonging to the noble sir to the boy.”
“Having asked for something else, we will give it to the Master.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to that family. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then that man approached the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son. Having approached... [the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son].
Having paid homage to Upananda the Sakyan-son, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the man said to the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan-son:
"Venerable sir, yesterday evening some meat was obtained. From that, a portion was set aside for the noble one."
“Venerable sir, this boy gets up at the time of dawn during the night and cries out, ‘Give me meat! The master’s share has been given to the boy.
Venerable sir, what should be brought for the kahāpaṇa?
“Friend, the kahāpaṇa has been relinquished by me.”
“Yes, venerable sir, it has been relinquished.
“Then, friend, give that very same kārṣāpaṇa to me.
Then that man, having given the kārṣāpaṇa to the Venerable Upananda the Śākyan, complained and criticized him.
He complained: “Just as we accept silver, so too do these recluses, the sons of the Sakyans, accept silver.
The monks heard that man complaining, criticizing, and complaining.
Those monks who were of few desires... [they] complained, criticized, and complained.
“How indeed could the venerable Upananda the Sakyan son accept silver?
Then those monks, having rebuked the venerable Upananda the Sakyan son in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Blessed One asked:
“Is it true, Upananda, that you accepted silver?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, foolish man, accept silver? This is not for one who has gone forth to do.”
“Monk, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
‘If any monk should take gold or silver, or cause it to be taken, or consent to its being deposited for him, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).’”
"But whoever" means whoever such as this...
"a bhikkhu."
...pe... this is the meaning intended here by the term "bhikkhu.
"Jātarūpa" (gold) is said to be that which has the color of a teacher (or the color of a wound).
"Silver" refers to the kahāpaṇa,
the copper māsaka, the wooden māsaka, the lac māsaka, and whatever else comes into common circulation.
"Should acquire" means...
If she takes it herself, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya pācittiya).
If she causes another to take it,
it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya pācittiya).
"Or he should accept what has been set down":
if he accepts what has been set down with the thought, "Let this be for the noble one," it is an offense of expiation (nissaggiya).
It must be relinquished in the midst of the Saṅgha.
And furthermore, monks, it should be relinquished in this way:

that monk, having approached the Saṅgha, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet of the elder monks, having sat down on his haunches and extended his hands in reverential salutation, should speak thus:
“Venerable sirs, I accepted silver.”
“This is my article to be relinquished; I relinquish it to the Saṅgha.
Having relinquished it, the offense is to be confessed.
An offense should be received by a competent monk who is capable.
If a monastery attendant or a lay follower arrives there, he should be told:
"Friend, please take note of this."
If he says, "What should be brought by this [person]?",
one should not say:
“Bring this or that. One should point out what is allowable:
ghee, oil, honey, or molasses.
If he exchanges it for something allowable and brings it back, then—with the exception of the one who accepted the money—it may be used by everyone.
If it can be obtained in this way, that is good;
if it cannot be obtained, he should be told:
“Friend, discard this.
If he discards it, that is well.
If he does not discard it, a monk endowed with five qualities should be appointed as the discarder of money:

"One who would not go astray through favoritism, nor go astray through ill will, nor go astray through delusion, nor go astray through fear, and who would know what has been discarded and what has not been discarded.
"And furthermore, monks, he is to be appointed in this way:
first, a monk is to be requested."
Having made a formal request, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should appoint the monk named so-and-so as the discarder of money.”
This is the motion.
Let the Sangha hear me, venerable sirs.
The Sangha appoints the monk named so-and-so as the discarder of silver.
Whichever venerable one approves of the appointment of the monk named so-and-so as the discarder of money, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The monk named so-and-so has been appointed by the Saṅgha as the discarder of money.
“The Saṅgha consents, therefore it is silent;
thus do I understand this.
That monk who has been appointed should drop [the stone] after making a mark.
If he causes it to fall after making a sign, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one perceives money as money and accepts money, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If one is in doubt regarding money and accepts money, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If one perceives what is not money as money and accepts it, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If one perceives what is not money as money, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one is in doubt regarding what is not money, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is formless and he perceives it as formless, there is no offense.
There is no offense if,
within a monastery or within a dwelling, he takes it up or has it taken up and then sets it aside.
"He who shall have it, he shall take it"— [this applies] to one who is insane,
or to a first offender.
The eighth training rule concerning silver is finished.
